Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
In his Tahdhīb, for example, Ibn ʿAsākir does not limit this Christian influence to the Umayyad period. He takes it back as far as the time of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He reports that while giving a sermon at al-Jābiya, ʿUmar said that God “guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
A Christian Catholicos was present—a Catholicos being a Christian ecclesiastical title that entered Arabic usage—and he muttered something in his own language.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
ʿUmar asked what he had said and was told that the Catholicos was saying: “God does not lead anyone astray.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Ibn ʿAsākir appears to have seen this report as an example of an indirect debate between “official” Islamic thought, which attributed human action to God, and Christian theology, which defended human choice and denied that God Himself causes people to go astray.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
From this point of view, exchanges of this kind would have been what first stirred discussion of divine decree among Muslims.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
We find the same idea in other Muslim historians who say that Maʿbad al-Juhanī was the first person to teach the doctrine of free will.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
According to them, he took the idea from—or was influenced by—a Christian named Sinsawayh, who had converted to Islam and then returned to Christianity, as Ibn Saʿd reports in his Ṭabaqāt.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
According to these historians, this Christian influence then passed from Maʿbad to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī in Iraq, and to Ghaylān al-Dimashqī in Syria.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If we take all these views together, we are left with the conclusion that the problem which, as these same researchers rightly say, had already begun stirring Arab thought in the time of the Prophet and later emerged in an especially sharp form under the Umayyad caliph Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, whose reign began in 106 AH/724 CE, is explained from a single source.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

That source is either abstract rational reflection, driven by what Macdonald calls the “philosophical necessity of the human mind”; or what Aḥmad Amīn means when he says that this question “occupied philosophers and religious thinkers in every age”; or else the influence of Christian theological thought.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

But limiting the question to this framework alone goes against historical reality. It also goes against the dialectical relationship between intellectual developments and social developments. That relationship exists objectively, whether researchers notice it or not.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

What is striking is that some of these same researchers, in their own studies of the problem of human freedom and divine decree, actually give us excellent material for seeing this relationship. But they present it only as historical information. They do not use it as the basis for a scientific analysis that would trace the problem back to its real roots in the society where it took its particular forms.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Take Goldziher, for example. As we saw earlier, he explains the rise of the Qadarite movement as an attempt to reconcile apparently conflicting passages in the Qurʾān. He stops there, without asking what forces lay behind this attempt. Yet elsewhere in the very same book, when he discusses the rise of the Murjiʾa, he uses a very different kind of explanation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Goldziher explains the Murjiʾa doctrine, and what he sees as its tolerance toward the Umayyads, by the political need for such a doctrine at that particular time. In the eyes of much of the Muslim community, he says, the Umayyads had seized power illegitimately. A doctrine was therefore needed which taught that judgment on a Muslim’s faith should be postponed and left to God. This would prevent Muslims from quickly declaring the Umayyads unbelievers and would postpone that judgment until God Himself decided it. Otherwise, such an immediate judgment by Muslims might encourage them to rise against their rulers.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Here Goldziher gives a sound explanation. He connects the Murjiʾa doctrine directly to the political circumstances in which it appeared.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But when he turns to the Qadarites, his treatment splits in two.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

On the one hand, he explains their origin simply as an attempt to reconcile passages in the Qurʾān. On the other hand, when he discusses the attitude of the Umayyad rulers toward the Qadarites, he says that the Umayyads hated those who defended human free choice. Their hostility, he adds, did not come from any dislike of theological debate as such. It came from their belief that the disappearance of the doctrine of divine compulsion would threaten their rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Yet Goldziher makes this observation separately from his discussion of how the Qadarite movement arose. He never makes it part of that explanation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

This last point gives us excellent material for seeing the social and political ground from which the Qadarite movement grew. But Goldziher does not use it when he explains the movement’s origins, even though he does exactly that when explaining the rise of the Murjiʾa.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Even more surprising is the response of a modern Arab scholar known for the depth and range of his analysis. He quotes Goldziher’s remarks about the attitude of the Umayyad rulers toward the Qadarite movement and then comments:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“There is no doubt that the Umayyad state benefited from the ideas of the determinists, who saw the Umayyad caliphate, and the oppression produced by it, as a divine decree that human beings had no power to resist or rebel against. But the connection between the theoretical principle of free will and its practical consequences was not something the Umayyad caliphs understood in the way Goldziher imagined. The sacrifice of Maʿbad or Ghaylān was not caused by fear that their rule might collapse. It was simply a campaign against a new religious innovation, carried out in the name of the religion whose guardians they had made themselves.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There are several problems with this comment.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
First, it accepts the basic point that the Umayyad state benefited from the views of the determinists, and it gives a realistic explanation for why.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If that is so, then the views of those who defended human choice—the Qadarites—must have meant more than simple opposition to the injustice of the Umayyad state. Those views also posed a serious danger to its power.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

If the Qadarite idea spread among the people, it opened a door of hope for those suffering under oppression. They would come to understand that this oppression was not a divine decree that they had no choice but to accept. Its removal could depend on their own will and choice, if they rose to resist it and put an end to it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

It is hard to believe that the Umayyad rulers could not see this danger. They were known for their political skill and for the care with which they protected their rule, especially at a time when opposition movements were becoming stronger and developing new intellectual weapons that could spread quickly.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Even some early Muslim writers support this view. Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār, for example, says that “the first person to openly preach compulsion was Muʿāwiya.” He adds that Muʿāwiya claimed that whatever he did happened by God’s decree and was created by God. In this way, he could use divine decree as an excuse for his actions, make people think he was right, and suggest that God Himself had appointed him as ruler and entrusted authority to him. ʿAbd al-Jabbār says that this idea later became widespread among the Umayyad kings.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Second, even if we accepted for the sake of argument that the Umayyad caliphs did not understand the connection between the theoretical principle and its practical consequences in the way Goldziher did—and that would hardly fit their reputation for political cunning—there is another point that requires no extraordinary insight into the connection between theory and practice.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The same researcher mentions it himself when he adds:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“But alongside their theoretical belief in free choice, the Qadarites also expressed opposition to the state.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
He gives the example of Khālid ibn Maʿdān, one of Maʿbad’s students, who said as his teacher was being taken away to be killed:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“The greatest calamity is when the rulers come from among them,”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Despite the depth we usually find in this researcher’s work, there is an attempt here to separate the Qadarites’ theoretical doctrine from their opposition to the state. It is almost as if he is saying that the Umayyads killed Maʿbad not because of Qadarite doctrine, but because he opposed the government.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Such a separation does not fit a sound method of research.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Dr ʿAbbās tries to support this distinction by referring to Khālid ibn Maʿdān’s remark about the Umayyads when he saw Maʿbad being taken to his death. He argues that Khālid did not say this because he was a Qadarite. Many people who believed in divine compulsion said similar things.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
But first, this explanation concerns Khālid ibn Maʿdān alone. Does it mean that the Umayyads killed Maʿbad because he was a Qadarite?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Second, what exactly does the argument prove?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Does it mean that opposition to Umayyad rule was not limited to the Qadarites and that many determinists also opposed the Umayyads?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The opponents of the Umayyads belonged to many different political parties and religious schools. Each had its own intellectual weapons for fighting Umayyad rule. The Qadarite doctrine was not the only intellectual weapon used against them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The determinists themselves were not one single group. Al-Shahrastānī lists three main kinds: the pure Jabriyya, the moderate Jabriyya, and those who allowed created human power some degree of influence over human action. He also divides the Najjāriyya, one branch among them, into three groups.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Another branch, the followers of Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr, held a particularly interesting position on political leadership. One of their principles stated:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“The imamate may belong to someone who is not from Quraysh. If a Qurashī and a Nabataean are both available, we should choose the Nabataean, because he has fewer supporters and weaker backing, and we can remove him more easily if he violates the religious law.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
The Muʿtazila also allowed the imam to come from outside Quraysh, but they did not go so far as to say that the Nabataean should be preferred over the Qurashī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
So there were determinists whose ideas posed an even greater danger to Umayyad rule than those of the Muʿtazila, even though the Muʿtazila adopted the Qadarite idea of human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The claim that the imam did not have to come from Quraysh—the Umayyads themselves being Qurashī—and that even a Nabataean could be preferred over a Qurashī posed a direct threat to the Umayyad caliphate. It is no exaggeration to say that this threat was even greater than the one posed by Qadarite doctrine.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

So saying that many determinists spoke about the Umayyads in the same way as Khālid ibn Maʿdān does not prove what Dr ʿAbbās wants it to prove. Not every determinist held ideas that suited Umayyad policy.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Even if we assumed that all the determinists thought alike, we could still say, first, that although their ideas might have suited Umayyad policy, the Jabriyya were not an Umayyad party and were not a political alliance supporting the Umayyad family.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
They were an independent group with their own religious, intellectual and political positions. Those positions did not simply reproduce the positions of the Umayyad state.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Otherwise, how could we explain the killing of Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, the leading figure of the “pure Jabriyya”?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

The Umayyads certainly did not kill Jahm because he believed in compulsion. They themselves supported that doctrine and protected it. They killed him because he joined those who rebelled against Umayyad rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Nothing in Jahm’s belief in compulsion required him to obey the Umayyads or prevented him from rising against them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

There is another. Despite his belief in compulsion, Jahm had a strongly rational tendency in his thinking, as we will see at the end of this chapter. The Umayyads were hostile to people with this kind of rational approach.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Second, does the fact that many determinists shared Khālid ibn Maʿdān’s hostility toward the Umayyads prove that Qadarite doctrine was not an intellectual expression of the interests of a social group, and therefore did not pose a danger to Umayyad rule?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Third, does it provide convincing evidence that the Umayyad rulers did not kill Maʿbad because he was a Qadarite, but only because he joined Ibn al-Ashʿath’s rebellion?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Before accepting that, would we not first need to know why Maʿbad opposed the Umayyads and why he joined Ibn al-Ashʿath against them?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

One further claim remains to be discussed: that the Umayyads killed Maʿbad and Ghaylān not because they feared for their rule, but because they were suppressing a new religious innovation in the name of the religion whose guardians they claimed to be.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There are several problems with this argument.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

First, the Umayyad caliphs—with the exception of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz—committed many serious and well-known religious violations and introduced innovations of their own. The fact that they presented themselves as guardians of religion did not stop them, nor did any wish to respect the religious feelings of ordinary Muslims.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Second, the doctrine of compulsion itself was, like Qadarite doctrine, regarded by Muslims as a “new innovation.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Most of the leading figures of the major schools of law and theology rejected it, from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Abū Ḥanīfa to Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Abū Ḥanīfa both rejected the extremes of Qadarite free choice and Jabriyya compulsion with the well-known formula:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
“No compulsion, no complete delegation, and no absolute empowerment,”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
followed by the rest of the familiar report attributed to Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

Then we come to the fourth great imam of Sunni Islam, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal (d. 241 AH / 855 CE). He wrote an entire work entitled Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmites concerning the Ambiguous Verses of the Qurʾān Which They Questioned and Interpreted Incorrectly.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal places the Jahmites alongside the heretics and refutes them together. In his eyes, therefore, they too were followers of religious innovation.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
So the doctrine of compulsion was regarded by most of the leading figures of the Islamic schools as a “new innovation,” just as Qadarite doctrine was.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Why, then, did the Umayyad caliphs persecute one innovation but not the other?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Why distinguish between one “innovation” and another if their real concern was simply to defend the religion whose guardians they claimed to be?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

A much better answer comes from one of the leading Muslim scholars of our own time. No one could reasonably doubt that he is a major conservative Islamic scholar, and he is certainly not someone who approaches Islamic history with our particular concern for connecting theoretical principles with practical circumstances.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Writing about the Muʿtazilite hatred of the Umayyad state, he says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“Perhaps the Muʿtazila inherited their hatred of the Umayyads from these teachers of theirs”—meaning Maʿbad al-Juhanī and Ghaylān al-Dimashqī among the Qadarites, and Jahm ibn Ṣafwān among the determinists. “The Umayyads, it seems, disliked the doctrine of free will not only for religious reasons but for political reasons as well, because compulsion served their policy. The result of the doctrine of compulsion was that God, who causes all things, had imposed the Umayyads on the people just as He imposed everything else. Their state existed by God’s decree and destiny, and people therefore had to submit to that decree and destiny. Jahm, although a determinist, joined those who rebelled against the Umayyads. He also held views which caused ordinary people to resent him, so Umayyad policy took advantage of the people’s hatred and killed him.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
As for Jahm and the views that made people resent him, we believe that this question goes beyond the problem of compulsion and leads us to the rational tendency for which Jahm was known.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Third, it is difficult for anyone studying the Umayyad period to accept the claim that the Umayyad caliphs did not fear that Qadarite doctrine might threaten their rule.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

When Qadarite doctrine appeared in connection with Maʿbad al-Juhanī, the Umayyad state was going through an intense crisis. Political, social, class and religious tensions between rulers and ruled had all become severe.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Ideas directed against the rulers therefore found a wide and powerful response among the populations living under Umayyad rule, whatever the precise religious form of those ideas might be.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Any idea that directly, or even indirectly, challenged some part of Umayyad rule could spread quickly among the people. It could attract preachers, supporters and even people willing to fight for it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
That is exactly what happened when Qadarite doctrine took its later form through Maʿbad al-Juhanī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Historical sources tell us that Maʿbad went to the Hijaz carrying his Qadarite message to a region whose people were generally more conservative in religious matters than the people of Iraq.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
There he met the scholars of Medina and explained his doctrine to them. The scholars of Medina were known for being among the strictest Muslim scholars on questions of religion and belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
What response did Maʿbad find among them?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

One of the great historians of Islamic beliefs gives us the answer. He was himself a major Sunni scholar and an opponent of Qadarite doctrine, yet he openly admits how widely the doctrine had spread at that time.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
Speaking specifically about the Qadarites, he says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

“…and among those who escaped these false doctrines, there remained only a small group from among the most distinguished scholars and the righteous early generations whom God protected from deviation and error…”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

He says this because the historical record tells us that Maʿbad influenced the scholars of Medina, who adopted his doctrine, just as he influenced many people in Iraq, a region strongly hostile to the Umayyads.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
This historical reality shows very clearly that the Qadarite idea could appeal even to conservative religious scholars who held great influence over public opinion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
So we have to ask: what was it about Qadarite doctrine that attracted these scholars and so many other people?
